rules.plain_language_rule: Rugby requires development of multiple physical qualities.
Training should consider both general rugby demands and position-specific demands.
Coaches should identify a player’s physical qualities before determining training priorities.
Physical qualities can compete, so programming requires prioritisation rather than maximising everything simultaneously.
Physical development should ultimately contribute to improved on-field performance.
Lifestyle factors outside formal training can affect training and game performance.
Coaches should maintain awareness of relevant external stresses and provide appropriate support/advice.
Physical preparation is one component of holistic rugby development alongside technical, tactical, and mental development.
S&C should prioritize physical characteristics that meaningfully support game performance.
Comparison with the general population can help identify characteristics associated with rugby participation.
Characteristics that distinguish higher playing levels may be especially valuable for player development.
Players should be compared with relevant competition-level benchmarks where reliable normative data exist.
Rugby physical profiles evolve as laws, playing styles, training practices, and game demands change.
Physical benchmarks must therefore be contextual rather than permanently fixed.
Athlete profiling should incorporate current ability, position, playing level, and development target.
A physical characteristic associated with elite performance should not automatically be maximized; the objective is an appropriate overall profile.
Body size includes stature and body mass and can influence rugby performance.
Increased body mass can improve resistance to displacement during contact.
Collision momentum depends on both mass and velocity.
Increasing velocity can increase momentum without increasing body mass.
Increased muscular mass can contribute to greater force-production capacity.
Body mass differs across playing levels and has increased historically as rugby has evolved.
Greater body mass is not automatically better.
The target should be functional body mass appropriate to the player’s position and game demands.
Changes in body mass should be interpreted alongside speed, strength, power, conditioning, and rugby performance.
The system should monitor longitudinal body-mass trends rather than relying only on single measurements.
Body mass alone should not be used as a proxy for injury protection or overall physical readiness.
